newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says no plan for French or Russian jets.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says no plan for French or Russian jets.

text.p: Indonesian Air Force chief Air Marshall Sutria Tubagus said on Thursday Jakarta had no plans to buy jet fighters from France or Russia.

Sutria denied media reports earlier this week that the air force was considering alternative suppliers after the United States delayed a sale of nine Lockheed Martin Corp F-16 jets because of Congressional concerns over Indonesia's human rights record.
"According to the air force's programme, we have no plans to buy fighter planes from France or Russia," Sutria told Reuters.
"We have in our programme to develop the air force using only certain fighters, including F-16 jets, in order to fulfil our goal of establising high-standard squadrons," Sutria said.
Indonesia bought 12 F-16 in 1986 and Sutria said he considered a full squadron to be made up of around 20 aircraft.
"The other programme is to buy Hawk jets from Britain. We have bought 24 Hawks. We have signed a deal with British Aerospace for an additional 16 Hawks," he said.
Indonesia bought the 24 Hawk 100 and 200 series jets from British Aerospace in 1993 and Sutria said 14 of the planes had already arrived in Indonesia.
"Next March, the delivery is expected to be concluded for the total 24 jets that we have ordered," he said.
"We expect first delivery of the additional (16) Hawks in 1998," he said.
The Clinton administration postponed the sale of at least nine F-16s until January because of Congressional objections to Jakarta's recent crackdown on political dissent.
Administration officials last month said they intended to go through with the sale of the jets.

In July, shortly after the Clinton administration agreed to sell the F-16s, Indonesia's military raided offices of an opposition party and arrested a number of political activists, a move which sparked the worst riots in Jakarta for more than 20 years.

Clinton first offered the nine F-16s to Indonesia in October 1995 as part of an effort to recoup the cost of the batch of 28 aircraft originally built and paid for by Pakistan. Congress blocked the sale to Pakistan in 1990 because of its suspected programme to develop nuclear weapons and Washington is seeking to sell the F-16s to other countries to reimburse $658 million to Pakistan.
